author: ChatGPT
title: The Alignment Lab — Discover eigenvectors
notice: CHATGPT-AUTHORED DRAFT — requires implementation and educational play review. Not yet an approved lesson.
objectives: Distinguish a matrix changing an arrow's direction from merely changing its length or reversing it.
Predict a concrete 2×2 matrix output before seeing the result, then connect it to direction.
Discover a non-zero eigendirection by active manipulation and verify it numerically.
Compute A v by row-by-vector multiplication; test whether A v = λ v using one scalar for both coordinates.
Identify a negative eigenvalue as reversal along the same line and recognise non-axis eigendirections.
Transfer the test to an unseen matrix without visual assistance.
successCriteria: Each of the seven challenge screens initially presents one task, one action and only enough information to attempt it; detailed teaching follows the response.
Challenge 1 requires a committed prediction before displaying the result. Challenge 2 asks the learner to compare direction using the dotted guide.
Challenge 3 requires the learner to move the teal dot and commit a non-zero horizontal solution; a zero vector is rejected with feedback only when attempted.
Challenge 4 requires a calculated result without revealing the transformed arrow first; feedback distinguishes x-only and y-only correctness.
Challenge 5 shows only the line-classification decision first, then the multiplier question, and correctly accepts a negative multiplier.
Challenge 6 first checks the TWO candidate directions, then reveals multiplier inputs for only those directions. No transformed arrows appear before full success.
Challenge 7 presents output calculation, scalar, and second-vector classification as three consecutive phases. No diagrams before full success.
Every learner-facing string, including newly required phase buttons and transitional feedback, is from this specification. No coder-generated teaching.
Real learning remains unverified until a learner can complete a later transfer task independently and reports the instructions clear.

steps.title: The Alignment Lab
body: A matrix changes an arrow. Most arrows turn. A few stay on the same straight line.

steps.title: What will the matrix do?
body: This matrix doubles x. It leaves y unchanged.

copy.graphDescription: A teal arrow runs from the origin to (2, 1). After the answer, an orange arrow appears to (4, 1). The arrows lie on different lines.
copy.hintText: For the new x, multiply 2 by the teal x coordinate. Keep y as it is.
copy.question: Where will the orange arrow end?
copy.feedbackA: Yes. x doubles from 2 to 4. y stays at 1.
copy.feedbackB: The matrix changes x. This answer leaves it unchanged.
copy.feedbackC: You've doubled y too. Only x doubles.
copy.feedbackD: Check which coordinate the matrix doubles.
copy.revealExplanation: Look at the arrows. The teal ends at (2, 1); the orange ends at (4, 1). The orange arrow has turned.
copy.a11yChoices: Choose where the orange arrow will end. It stays hidden until the correct choice.
copy.a11yReveal: The orange arrow ends at (4, 1), off the original teal line.

steps.title: Did it turn?
body: The dotted line follows the teal arrow.

copy.graphDescription: The dotted line follows the teal arrow through (2, 1). The orange arrow ends at (4, 1), below that line.
copy.hintText: Follow the dotted line past the teal arrow. Does it reach the orange tip?
copy.question: Is the orange arrow on that line?
copy.choiceC: They are exactly the same arrow
copy.feedbackA: Look at the orange tip. It sits below the dotted line.
copy.feedbackB: Correct. The orange tip is off the dotted line.
copy.feedbackC: The tips are at different places, and the arrows point at different angles.
copy.revealExplanation: When the result leaves the original line, the matrix has changed the arrow's direction.
copy.a11yChoices: A line extends through the teal arrow and the origin. Is the orange arrow on it?
copy.a11yReveal: The orange arrow is not on the teal arrow's line.

steps.title: Make the arrows line up
body: Move the teal dot. Watch the orange arrow.

copy.graphDescription: Move the teal arrow's tip across whole-number grid points. The orange arrow changes with it. The dotted line follows the teal arrow through the origin.
copy.hintText: Try making the teal y coordinate zero. What changes?
copy.question: Can you get the orange arrow onto the dotted line?
copy.feedbackZero: The dot is at the origin. Move it away from (0, 0) and try again.
copy.feedbackTurned: Not yet. The orange arrow is still off the dotted line.
copy.feedbackCorrect: Yes. Both arrows are on the same line.
copy.revealExplanation: Here the matrix adds y to x. When y is zero, the arrow doesn't change. Every non-zero horizontal arrow works.
copy.a11yChoices: Drag the teal dot or change x and y. Make the orange arrow share the teal line, then press Check.
copy.a11yReveal: Non-zero horizontal arrows work: y equal to zero makes the matrix leave the arrow unchanged.

steps.title: Work it out before looking
body: The orange arrow is hidden. The top matrix row gives its x. The bottom row gives its y.

copy.graphDescription: A teal arrow ends at (2, 1). The orange arrow stays hidden until the calculation is correct, then appears at (3, 1).
copy.question: Where will the orange arrow end?
copy.feedbackInvalid: Enter a number in each box.
copy.feedbackXOnly: x is right. Use the bottom row to find y.
copy.feedbackYOnly: y is right. Use the top row to find x.
copy.feedbackNeither: Use one matrix row for x, then the other row for y.
copy.feedbackCorrect: Correct. The orange arrow ends at (3, 1).
copy.revealExplanation: Top row gives 3. Bottom row gives 1. The result is (3, 1), not a multiple of (2, 1). The arrow turns.
copy.a11yChoices: Enter the two coordinates of the hidden orange arrow. A hint is available after an incorrect attempt.
copy.a11yReveal: The input (2, 1) becomes (3, 1). The arrows lie on different lines.

steps.title: What if an arrow flips?
body: The teal arrow points right. The orange arrow points left.

copy.graphDescription: The teal arrow ends at (1, 0), pointing right. The orange ends at (-2, 0), pointing left. Both lie on the same horizontal line.
copy.hintText: A minus sign reverses an arrow. Compare the two arrow lengths.
copy.lineQuestion: Are they on the same straight line?
copy.scaleQuestion: What number turns the teal arrow into the orange one?
copy.feedbackWrongLine: Follow the horizontal line through the origin. Does it reach both tips?
copy.feedbackPositiveScale: A positive number keeps the arrow pointing right. We need left.
copy.feedbackWrongScale: Compare the lengths, then check the sign.
copy.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Multiply the teal arrow by −2 to get the orange one.
copy.revealExplanation: An eigenvector stays on its original line when a matrix acts on it. The multiplier is its eigenvalue. Here the eigenvalue is −2: the arrow reverses and doubles.
copy.a11yChoices: First decide whether both arrows lie on one line. Then enter the multiplier.
copy.a11yReveal: The orange arrow is -2 times the teal arrow. The eigenvalue is negative.
copy.lineCorrectText: Yes. They point opposite ways, but share the same line.

steps.title: Which directions survive?
body: Two of these four arrows stay on their original lines.

copy.graphDescription: Four teal arrows: A (1, 1), B (1, -1), C (2, 1) and D (1, 0). After success, A ends at (3, 3) and B ends at (1, -1).
copy.hintText: Try A. Multiply the matrix by (1, 1). Can one number turn the input into the result?
copy.question: Which two?
copy.feedbackContainsC: C turns. Its two coordinates would need different multipliers.
copy.feedbackContainsD: D turns. Its output no longer lies along the x-axis.
copy.feedbackWrongScaleA: A is a correct direction. Check how much it stretches.
copy.feedbackWrongScaleB: B is a correct direction. Check whether its length changes.
copy.feedbackCorrect: Yes. Both directions stay on their original lines.
copy.revealExplanation: A = (1, 1) becomes (3, 3): eigenvalue 3. B = (1, −1) stays (1, −1): eigenvalue 1. Eigenvectors can point diagonally too.
copy.a11yChoices: First choose two candidate arrows. Then enter their multipliers. Results stay hidden until both multipliers are right.
copy.a11yReveal: A stretches by 3. B stays unchanged with multiplier 1.
copy.directionCorrectText: Both directions work. Now find their multipliers.

steps.title: Try it without the diagram
body: Calculate first. The arrows will appear at the end.

copy.graphDescription: First diagram: (2, 0) becomes (6, 0) on the same horizontal line. Second: (1, 1) becomes (3, 2), which turns off the diagonal.
copy.hintText: Use one matrix row per output coordinate. To test direction, check whether one multiplier works for both coordinates.
copy.partAScaleQuestion: What number multiplies the whole vector?
copy.partBQuestion: Does (1, 1) stay on its original line?
copy.feedbackWrongOutput: Check the top row for x and the bottom row for y.
copy.feedbackWrongScale: Compare the output with the input. What one number takes you from one to the other?
copy.feedbackWrongClassification: Calculate the output of (1, 1). Does one multiplier work for x and y?
copy.feedbackCorrect: Correct. You worked it out without the picture.
copy.revealExplanation: (2, 0) becomes (6, 0), so its eigenvalue is 3. But (1, 1) becomes (3, 2): no single multiplier works for both coordinates.
copy.a11yChoices: First calculate the output for (2, 0). Then find its multiplier. Finally decide whether (1, 1) keeps its direction. No diagram appears before success.
copy.a11yReveal: (2, 0) becomes (6, 0), eigenvalue 3. (1, 1) becomes (3, 2) and is not an eigenvector.
copy.outputCorrectText: The output is right. Now compare it with the input.

steps.title: The key idea
body: A non-zero vector is an eigenvector when the matrix leaves it on the same straight line.
The number that stretches, shrinks or reverses it is the eigenvalue: A v = λ v.
Want to test yourself again? Try without hints.
